concepts.name: Let no sin rule over me
concepts.why: All nine: only Gen 4:7 says 'crouching at your door'; Ps 19:13, Ps 119:133, Rom 6:12 and Rom 6:16 and John 8:34 say sin rules, reigns and enslaves. A name that one passage says and the others do not. 'Let no sin rule over me' (Ps 119:133) fits every passage, including Gen 4:7's 'you must master it'.

Secular/academic and biblical-theological readers: Num 14:9 is Caleb and Joshua's exhortation 'do not rebel', not a report that they rebelled; it shares the word without holding the concept. Deut 9:7 already carries the wilderness rebellion.

Reformed, Wesleyan, Catholic, Orthodox, Baptist: the name is Paul's cry of someone who wants the good and does not do it (Rom 7:18-19, 7:23, Gal 5:17). Jer 13:23 (accustomed to evil, not able) and Rom 8:7 (hostile to God, cannot submit) say nothing of wanting the good, so they do not hold this name; bundling them with Rom 7 and Gal 5:17 (written to believers) is the very 'inability' grouping where the traditions part, and the drafter said the name was chosen to avoid it. Move them to their own concept (see missing: 'Neither are you able to do good').

note_fixes: Proverbs 20:9: the note as written says the opposite of the verse; quote the whole question: 'Who can say, “I have kept my heart pure; I am cleansed from my sin”?'
concepts.why: Secular/academic and every reader of the note alone: 'I have kept my heart pure; I am cleansed from my sin' is a claim the verse asks who could make.

concepts.name: The fathers, the children, and each one's own iniquity
concepts.why: Reformed, Wesleyan, Catholic, Orthodox, secular and Jewish readers of the Hebrew Bible: the name gives only one voice ('the iniquity of the fathers on the children') while three of the seven passages (Deut 24:16, Jer 31:29-30, Ezek 18:20) say the opposite. The drafter keeps both voices side by side, so the name should not state either as the claim. A plain label that holds both.

Reformed, Wesleyan, Baptist (eternal security): Heb 6:8 is a figure for those who fall away inside the Hebrews 6 warning, a passage the traditions read in opposite ways. It shares 'thorns and thistles' and 'curse' with Gen 3:17-18 but does not say the ground is cursed because of man; set under 'Cursed is the ground' it is read as a literal echo and the apostasy question is imported silently.

Secular/academic and biblical-theological readers: Heb 9:27 says man is appointed to die once and then judgment; it does not say dust or return. Put it with the universality of death (see missing: 'What man can live and never see death?').

Secular/academic and biblical-theological readers: 2 Kgs 13:23 says the LORD was unwilling to cast Israel from His presence, the opposite of the name, and its note quotes that denial. It is a word of grace and belongs in the last concept (Israel not cast off for the covenant's sake).
Secular/academic reader: the name says 'among the nations' (Hos 9:17, Deut 28:65, Lam 1:3); Gen 4:12 is Cain a wanderer on the earth, and it is already in 'Cursed is the ground' (Gen 4:11-12).

secondary_or_links: Concept 31 (last, hope): it is the theme's own words of hope and covers all three: sin (Isa 40:2 pardoned, Rom 5:20), exile (Deut 30:3-4, Ezek 36:24), death (Isa 25:8, Ezek 37:12, Rom 6:23, 1 Cor 15:54-55), and keeps the double for all her sins in Isa 40:2. I found nothing dark softened or left out to make room; the dark concepts keep Sheol's silence (21), Ps 137 grief (30), 'He gave them over' (16) and the hidden face (26) untouched. Add 2 Kgs 13:23 (moved from 25) here if the owner wants a word of grace for Israel in the exile strand. The name is Rom 5:20; the OT passages under it do not say 'grace', and Jewish/secular and dispensational readers may feel Ezek 36 and 37 (land and graves) are set beside 1 Cor 15 as one hope; no concept says one fulfils the other, so I accept, but keep the notes strictly to the verses' own words.

Concept 2: Rev 12:9 is the only place the serpent is named the devil; Genesis does not. Its words are the text's own, so it may stay, but a Jewish or secular reader will see it as the one passage that identifies the serpent. If the owner prefers the neutral line, drop it and leave it to the Spiritual Warfare link.

Concept 8: Exod 20:3-4 and 1 Kgs 12:28 / Isa 44:17 do not say 'forsaken Me' as the name does (they command, or describe calf and idol worship); acceptable because all concern other gods and images, but if tightened the plain label 'Other gods and idols' would hold them all.

Secondary 'Sin -> wash me clean': Jer 2:22 says washing does not remove the stain; it is the other voice, not an instance of being washed clean. Fine if kept, but it does not hold the name as the Ps 51 and Isa 1 passages do.
Links: 'Law/Wisdom' and 'Wisdom Literature' both appear; check they are two distinct themes and not one listed twice.

missing.sub_theme: Sinful from birth (the texts' words: 'brought forth in iniquity', 'estranged from birth')
missing.why: Where the traditions part most (original sin) and the drafter deliberately left Ps 51:5 out. Leaving the verses out of the theme is not neutral: these are the texts' own dark words on the origin of sin and a reader of this theme will look for them. Give them as plain quotation with no gloss, as the site does for 'Sin entered the world through one man'.

missing.sub_theme: What man can live and never see death?
missing.why: The universality of death is plainly developed and is currently only implied by 'To dust you shall return', where Heb 9:27 does not fit.

The darkest word on death in the canon is absent, while the hope concept has death swallowed up. The traditions part on what it means (annihilation, eternal punishment, last-things order), so give the words only; the Judgment link alone does not carry it.

missing.sub_theme: All this came upon us, though we had not forgotten You
missing.why: The drafter left Ps 44:11 out because the people claim innocence. That is the other voice on exile and death, kept for fathers and children in concept 15 but dropped here; without it every exile text in the outline is retribution, which a secular or Jewish reader of the Hebrew Bible will see as one-sided.

missing.sub_theme: Neither are you able to do good
missing.why: Where these two verses go once removed from concept 11; they hold a different claim (not able, hostile to God) from Paul's 'I want the good and do not do it'. Plain quotation, no word on who can or cannot, which is where the traditions part.
